title: Thermodynamic systems: closed, open and isolated, with properties and state

parts.label: Piston
parts.ask: Why is the piston part of the boundary?

explain.say: Put your thumb over the end of a bicycle pump and push. The trapped air gets squeezed and warm. To study it, thermodynamics first draws a boundary around exactly what we care about, the air, and calls it the system. Everything else is the surroundings. Look at the gas under the piston.

draw.text: Thermodynamic systems: closed, open and isolated, with properties and state

parts.label: Piston
parts.ask: Why is the piston part of the boundary?

draw.text: System: the stuff inside the boundary. Surroundings: everything else

explain.say: Systems come in three kinds. A closed system lets energy cross its boundary but no mass, like gas trapped under a piston. See the closed group? A tyre is closed too. Can heat still flow into a closed system?

draw.name: x-sort
draw.question: Which kind of system is it?

draw.text: Closed: energy crosses, mass does not

explain.say: Yes, heat and work can cross. An open system, or control volume, lets mass flow through as well, like steam rushing through a turbine. An isolated system lets nothing cross, neither mass nor energy; a perfect thermos flask comes close. Which kind is a car radiator?

draw.name: x-sort
draw.question: Which kind of system is it?

draw.text: Open: mass flows in and out. Isolated: nothing crosses

explain.say: Open, coolant flows through it. Now properties, the numbers that describe the system. Cut the system in half: temperature and pressure stay the same in each half, so they are intensive. Mass, volume and energy halve, so they are extensive. See the two columns? Is density intensive?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Cut a system in two: intensive stays the same

draw.text: Specific volume v = V / m turns extensive into intensive

explain.say: Yes! The state is the condition described by all the properties. For a simple gas, two independent properties fix the state. For example, 1 kilogram of air at 300 kelvin and 100 kilopascals must fill 0.861 cubic metres, from P V equals m R T. Well done! Exam tip: always draw and name your system boundary first.

parts.label: Piston
parts.ask: Why is the piston part of the boundary?

faq.a: It is the quantity of matter or region of space you choose to study, separated from its surroundings by a boundary, real or imagined.

faq.q: Why is the piston part of the boundary?
faq.a: The piston can move, so the boundary of the gas moves with it. When it moves out, the gas does work on the surroundings. A boundary can move without letting mass cross.

faq.q: What is the difference between an open and a closed system?
faq.a: A closed system lets energy cross its boundary but not mass. An open system, also called a control volume, lets mass flow in and out as well, like a turbine or pump.

faq.q: What are intensive and extensive properties?
faq.a: Intensive properties, like temperature and pressure, do not depend on the amount of matter. Extensive properties, like mass, volume and energy, scale with the size of the system.

faq.q: What does the state of a system mean?
faq.a: The state is the condition of the system described by its properties. For a simple compressible substance, two independent intensive properties fix the state; this is the state postulate.

facts: A closed system exchanges energy but not mass with its surroundings.
The gas constant of air is about 0.287 kilojoules per kilogram kelvin.

wrong.1: That is for 1 kilogram; the mass is 2 kilograms.

quiz.say: Which of these is an intensive property?
quiz.why: Temperature does not change if you cut the system in half.

wrong.1: Volume halves when the system is halved, so it is extensive.
wrong.2: Total internal energy scales with mass, so it is extensive.
